v: Know the four parts and how long each takes
Choose Academic or General Training
Understand band scores and how the overall band is worked out
Academic – for university study and many professional registrations (doctors, nurses, engineers)
General Training – for work, training and most immigration routes (for example Canada, Australia, the UK work visa)
Listening and Speaking are the same in both. Reading and Writing are different.

b.v: Check the exact test and band your university, employer or visa asks for before you book. Booking the wrong one is the most expensive mistake in IELTS.

v: Listening – about 30 minutes, 4 recordings, 40 questions
Reading – 60 minutes, 3 sections, 40 questions
Writing – 60 minutes, 2 tasks
Speaking – 11 to 14 minutes, face to face with an examiner, 3 parts

b.v: Listening, Reading and Writing are taken together on one day. Speaking may be the same day or up to a week before or after.
Each part gets a band from 0 to 9, in half bands (5.0, 5.5, 6.0 …). The overall band is the average of the four, rounded to the nearest half band.

v: an average of 6.25 rounds up to 6.5
an average of 6.75 rounds up to 7.0
an average of 6.125 rounds down to 6.0
5 – modest user: copes with overall meaning, makes many mistakes
6 – competent user: effective, with some inaccuracies
7 – good user: handles complex language well, occasional errors
8 – very good user: only rare, unsystematic errors

b.v: Many universities ask for 6.5 overall with no part below 6.0. Plan for the lowest part, not the average.

day-2.t: Day 2 — Listening: format and core skills

v: Know what each of the four recordings is like
Read ahead and predict answers
Avoid the traps that cost easy marks
Part 1 – a conversation in an everyday situation (booking, registering, enquiring)
Part 2 – one person speaking about an everyday topic (a tour, a local facility)
Part 3 – a conversation in a study setting (students and a tutor)
Part 4 – a short lecture on an academic subject

b.v: You hear each recording once only. There is no replay.

v: Underline the key word in each question
Predict the kind of answer: a number, a name, a date, a noun, an adjective?
Check the word limit: 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER'
Notice the order – answers come in the same order as the questions
Distractors: the speaker gives one answer, then corrects it ('Tuesday – oh no, sorry, Thursday')
Spelling: a misspelt answer is wrong. Names are often spelt out – practise the alphabet
Numbers: 13 and 30, 15 and 50 sound close – listen for the stress
Plurals: 'book' when the answer is 'books' can lose the mark
Word limit: three words when the limit is two is marked wrong
about 16/40 → band 5.5
about 23/40 → band 6.0
about 30/40 → band 7.0
about 35/40 → band 8.0

b.v: The exact table changes slightly from test to test, but these are a good guide for practice.

Listen to any English news clip for 3 minutes and write down every number and name you hear.|Check your spelling against the transcript or subtitles.|Repeat daily for a week – your accuracy will climb quickly.

v: Handle form, note and table completion
Answer multiple choice without falling for paraphrase traps
Follow a map or plan

b.v: These are the most common questions, especially in Part 1. You fill gaps with words you hear.

v: Write exactly what you hear – do not change the word form
Dates can be written 12 March or March 12
Use capital letters for the whole answer on the computer test if you are unsure about capitals – capitals are always accepted

b.v: The recording rarely uses the same words as the options. It paraphrases. Often all three options are mentioned, but only one answers the question.

v: Question: 'Why did the student choose the course?'
A. It was cheap  B. A friend recommended it  C. It fitted her timetable
Recording: 'Honestly, the fee wasn't the issue, and my friend actually took a different one. It just happened to be the only one that didn't clash with my lectures.'
Answer: C – 'didn't clash with my lectures' = 'fitted her timetable'
Find the starting point before the recording begins
Learn direction language: opposite, next to, at the far end, on your left as you enter, just past, in the corner
Turn the map in your mind as the speaker moves

b.v: You match items (people, places, opinions) to a list of options. Some options are not used. Read the options carefully before the part starts.
Make your own paraphrase list.|expensive → costly, not cheap, a lot of money|start → begin, launch, open|problem → issue, difficulty, challenge|Add five new pairs every day.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Reading: skimming, scanning and timing

v: Read fast enough to finish
Find answers without reading every word
Manage 60 minutes for 40 questions

b.v: 1) What the Reading test looks like

v: Academic – three long passages from books, journals and magazines
General Training – shorter everyday texts (adverts, notices), then workplace texts, then one longer passage
40 questions, 60 minutes, and no extra time to copy answers

b.v: On the paper test there is no transfer time for Reading. Write answers straight onto the answer sheet.

v: Read the title and any subheadings
Read the first and last sentence of each paragraph
Write a 3-word summary next to each paragraph
Spend 2–3 minutes on this, not 10
Pick a word from the question that is easy to spot: a name, a number, a date, a capital letter
Move your eyes quickly down the text looking only for that
Then read the sentences around it carefully
Section 1: 17 minutes
Section 2: 20 minutes
Section 3: 23 minutes (it is the hardest)
If one question takes more than 2 minutes, guess, mark it and move on
Never leave a blank – there is no penalty for a wrong answer
about 23/40 → band 6.0
about 27/40 → band 6.5
about 30/40 → band 7.0
about 35/40 → band 8.0

b.v: General Training needs more correct answers for the same band, because its texts are easier.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Reading: True / False / Not Given and headings

v: Tell False from Not Given
Match headings to paragraphs
Practise on a real-style passage
TRUE – the text says the same thing
FALSE – the text says the opposite
NOT GIVEN – the text does not say, either way

b.v: For opinion passages the answers are YES / NO / NOT GIVEN. The logic is exactly the same.
Do not use your own knowledge. If the text does not say it, the answer is NOT GIVEN – even if it is true in real life.

Passage: The city's first public library opened in 1902 with fewer than 2,000 books. It was funded by a local merchant, who also paid the librarian's salary for the first ten years. Today the library holds over half a million items, and its reading rooms are among the busiest in the country.

v: 1. The library opened in the early twentieth century. → TRUE (1902)
2. The library was paid for by the city council. → FALSE (a local merchant paid)
3. The first librarian was a woman. → NOT GIVEN (the text does not say)
4. The library's reading rooms are the busiest in the country. → NOT GIVEN (it says 'among the busiest', not 'the busiest')
Read the paragraph first, then the headings – not the other way round
A heading matches the main idea of the whole paragraph, not one detail
Watch for headings that repeat a word from the paragraph – that is often a trap
There are always more headings than paragraphs

b.v: 4) Other question types you will meet

v: sentence and summary completion – check the word limit
matching information – which paragraph contains a detail
multiple choice – eliminate the wrong options first
diagram and flow-chart completion
Write a clear report on a chart (Academic) or a letter (General)
Always include an overview
Use the language of change and comparison
At least 150 words – fewer loses marks
Spend about 20 minutes on it
Task 1 is worth half as much as Task 2

b.v: You get a line graph, bar chart, pie chart, table, map or process. Describe the main features – do not give opinions or reasons.

v: Paragraph 1 – paraphrase the question in one sentence
Paragraph 2 – the overview: the two or three biggest trends (this is the paragraph most people forget)
Paragraphs 3–4 – details with numbers, grouped logically

b.v: No overview = no band 7 for Task Achievement, however good the rest is.

v: rose / increased / climbed – fell / decreased / dropped
sharply, steadily, slightly, dramatically
peaked at, reached a low of, remained stable at, fluctuated
twice as many as, a quarter of, the highest proportion, just over / just under

b.v: Example: 'Overall, car use rose steadily over the period, while bus travel fell by almost half.'

v: Three bullet points in the question – cover all three
Formal (Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully), semi-formal (Dear Mr Khan … Yours sincerely) or informal (Dear Ali … Best wishes)
Say why you are writing in the first sentence

b.v: Find any bar or line chart in a newspaper.|Write one sentence that paraphrases its title.|Write a two-sentence overview of the biggest trends.|Add four sentences of detail with numbers. Count your words.

v: Recognise the five essay types
Plan in five minutes
Write a four-paragraph essay that answers the question
At least 250 words
Spend about 40 minutes
It counts double – do it first if you run short of time
Opinion – 'To what extent do you agree or disagree?'
Discussion – 'Discuss both views and give your own opinion'
Advantages and disadvantages
Problem and solution (or cause and solution)
Two-part question – answer both parts
Introduction – paraphrase the topic and give your answer or position clearly
Body 1 – one main idea, explained, with an example
Body 2 – a second main idea, explained, with an example
Conclusion – sum up your position in two sentences, no new ideas
Task Response – did you answer every part of the question, with a clear position?
Coherence and Cohesion – logical paragraphs and linking
Lexical Resource – range and accuracy of vocabulary
Grammatical Range and Accuracy – a mix of simple and complex sentences, few errors

b.v: Memorised phrases like 'In this modern era of globalisation' do not raise your band. Examiners recognise them. Clear, accurate English does.

Question: 'Some people think children should start school at a very young age. Others think they should start later. Discuss both views and give your opinion.'|Write your position in one sentence.|Note one reason for each view, with an example.|Write the essay in 40 minutes, then count the words.

v: Know what happens in each part
Plan a two-minute talk in one minute
Sound fluent without memorising

b.v: Simple questions about you: home, work or study, hobbies, daily life. Give two or three sentences, not one word, not a speech.

v: Q: Do you like cooking?
Weak: 'Yes.'
Good: 'Yes, quite a lot. I usually cook on weekends – mostly Pakistani dishes like daal and rice, because they remind me of home.'
You get a card with a topic and three or four points
1 minute to prepare – write key words, not sentences
Speak for 1 to 2 minutes – keep going until the examiner stops you
Follow the points on the card in order – it gives you a structure

b.v: Deeper, more general questions linked to the Part 2 topic. Give an opinion, a reason and an example. It is fine to think aloud: 'That's an interesting question …'

v: Fluency and Coherence – speaking at length without long pauses
Lexical Resource – the range of words you use
Grammatical Range and Accuracy
Pronunciation – being easy to understand (an accent is fine)

b.v: If you do not understand a question, ask: 'Sorry, could you repeat the question?' This costs nothing.

Cue card: Describe a place you like to visit. You should say: where it is – how often you go – what you do there – and explain why you like it.|Set a timer for 1 minute and write key words.|Record yourself speaking for 2 minutes on your phone.|Listen back: count long pauses and repeated words.

day-9.t: Day 9 — Vocabulary, grammar and common mistakes

v: Fix the mistakes that hold Pakistani and Indian candidates at band 6
Use linking words correctly
Learn collocations, not single words
'discuss about the issue' → 'discuss the issue'
'return back' → 'return'
'cope up with' → 'cope with'
'do a mistake' → 'make a mistake'
'people is' → 'people are'
'I am having a car' → 'I have a car'
'Myself Khalid' → 'My name is Khalid'
'He is more better' → 'He is better'
missing articles: 'I went to university to study medicine' is right; 'I am student' → 'I am a student'

b.v: 2) Linking words – use them, do not overuse them

v: adding: moreover, in addition, furthermore
contrast: however, on the other hand, whereas, although
result: as a result, therefore, consequently
example: for example, for instance, such as

b.v: Starting every sentence with a linking word lowers your Coherence score. Two or three per paragraph is plenty.

v: make a decision, take responsibility, pay attention
a heavy burden, a growing concern, a significant impact
raise awareness, tackle a problem, meet a demand
strongly agree, highly unlikely, widely accepted
conditionals: If governments invested more, fewer people would …
relative clauses: Students who work part-time often …
passive voice: The data was collected in 2020 …
but accuracy matters more than complexity – a correct simple sentence beats a broken long one

b.v: Write five sentences about your city.|Use one conditional, one relative clause and one passive.|Check each against the mistake list above.

day-10.t: Day 10 — Test day and your study plan

v: Book the right test
Know what to bring and expect
Follow a four-week plan to your target band
Book through an official IELTS provider – the British Council or IDP
Choose computer-delivered or paper-based – the questions and difficulty are the same
Computer results usually arrive within a few days, paper results in about two weeks
Book four to six weeks ahead, especially before university intakes

b.v: Buy the test only from the official providers. Anyone offering a guaranteed band or a certificate without the test is a fraud.

v: Bring the same passport or ID you used to book – no ID, no test
Arrive early; phones and watches are collected
Paper test: write in pencil for Listening and Reading
Use the last minutes to check spelling and word limits
Week 1 – one full practice test to find your weakest part; daily Listening (30 min)
Week 2 – Reading every day with a timer; one Task 1 and one Task 2 essay
Week 3 – Writing every other day; Speaking recordings daily; review your mistake list
Week 4 – two more full timed tests; rest the day before the exam

b.v: Practise with the official Cambridge IELTS practice books or the free sample tests on the official IELTS website – they match the real test most closely.
4) The five habits of high scorers

v: They answer the exact question asked
They check spelling and word limits
They always write an overview in Task 1
They speak in full answers with reasons and examples
They practise under real time limits
